chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Fazzal, from Yunus ibn Yaqoub, from his maternal uncle Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Saeed al-Samman, who said:

I used to perform Hajj every year. When it was a difficult year in which people faced hardship, my companions said to me, 'If you were to consider what you intend to use for this year's Hajj and give it in charity, that would be superior.' I said to them, 'And you think that?' They said, 'Yes.' So I gave in charity that year what I intended to use for Hajj, and I stayed (at home). I saw a dream on the night of Arafat, and I said, 'By Allah, I will neither repeat it nor leave Hajj.'

He said: So when it was the following year, I performed Hajj. When I arrived at Mina, I saw Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and people were gathered around him. I went to him and said, 'Inform me about the man,' and I recounted my story to him, saying, 'Which of the two is superior: Hajj or charity?' He said, 'How good is the charity,' three times.

I said, 'Yes, but which of the two is superior?' He said, 'What prevents one of you from performing Hajj and giving charity?' I said, 'His wealth does not reach that, nor is it sufficient.' He said, 'If he intends to spend ten dirhams on something from the expenses of Hajj, he should spend five and give five in charity, or reduce something from his Hajj expenses and make what he withholds a charity, for he will have a reward for that.'

I said, 'If we did this, it would be correct.' He then said, 'And how is it like Hajj?' He said it three times: 'The servant goes out from his house, giving a portion, until he arrives at the Sacred Mosque, performs the obligatory Tawaf, then turns to the Station of Ibrahim and prays two cycles. An angel comes to him and stands at his left. When he finishes, the angel strikes his shoulder and says, 'O you! As for what has passed, it has been forgiven for you, and as for what is to come, strive.'
ai.seo_question: Which is better: performing Hajj or giving charity, according to Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him)?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi highlights the Shia scholarly view that while charity is virtuous, the ritual completeness of Hajj holds unique spiritual weight, as evidenced by the Imam’s triple emphasis on its merit. The narration introduces a practical jurisprudential nuance: if resources are limited, one should not abandon Hajj entirely but rather allocate a portion of the travel budget to charity, balancing ritual obligation with voluntary piety. The concluding vision of the angel promising forgiveness for past sins underscores the Hajj’s role as a comprehensive spiritual reset, a concept deeply rooted in Shia devotional practice.
